title: Failure File: averaging down a loser
hook: Down 28% from its high. Bargain, right?
takeaway: Averaging down means buying more as a stock falls. In Cisco's 2000-2002 fall, a buyer adding $10,000 after every further 20% drop had $50,000 in by March 2001, worth about $17,500 at the 2002 low. Each buy went into a trade already losing. One buy with a stop 8% below it would have cost about $800. Never add to a loser.
learn: Averaging down means buying more of a stock as it falls.
In Cisco's 2000 to 2002 fall, five $10,000 buys turned $50,000 into about $17,500 at the low.
Every new buy went into a trade that was already losing, so one bad trade became five times bigger.
One buy with a stop 8% below it would have cost about $800: never add to a loser.
emotion: "oh no, that's me": the slow sink of a 'bargain' that keeps getting cheaper

captions: Down 28% from its high. Bargain, right?
Weeks earlier it was the world's most valuable company.
Every 20% lower, our buyer added another $10,000.
By October 2002 it was down 88% from the top.
The clues were there. Every bounce topped out lower.
And every new buy went into a trade already losing.

props.fact: It lowers your average price. It [[raises]] what you can lose.

captions: Buying more as it falls is called averaging down.
It lowers your average price. And grows the bet.
One buy and a stop 8% below it? Out for $800.
Never add to a loser. Livermore and O'Neil agree.

sources.title: Yahoo Finance: Cisco Systems (CSCO) price history, via yfinance (split- and dividend-adjusted)
sources.used_for: weekly closes 1999-06 to 2003-06; high in the week of 2000-03-24; buys computed by the rule (first at −28% on 2000-04-14, then 2000-12-22, 2001-02-09, 2001-03-02, 2001-03-30); low week 2002-10-04 (−88%); value of the five buys at the low $17,542; an 8% stop under the first buy hit on the week of 2000-10-27 (about −$800, assuming a fill at the stop)

sources.used_for: in late March 2000 Cisco became the most valuable company in the world, over $500 billion; it lost about 80% of its value by 2002

sources.title: Jesse L. Livermore, How to Trade in Stocks (1940), ch. II (first-edition record: Bauman Rare Books)
sources.used_for: never average losses; no second trade if the first shows a loss

sources.title: Wikipedia: CAN SLIM (William O'Neil)
sources.used_for: cut all losses at no more than 7% or 8% below the buy point, with no exceptions
